---
title: "feature engineering"
---

## check the distribution before transforming

- before choosing imputation, encoding, or scaling, look at what each feature actually is and how it's shaped — the right transformation depends on both, not on a default pipeline applied to every column the same way
- plot distributions first: a histogram or kde for continuous features, value counts for categorical ones, and a boxplot or iqr check for outliers; a skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal distribution needs different handling than a roughly symmetric one
- skewness gives a quick numeric read on shape: a long right tail (common in income, lab counts, time-to-event data) often benefits from a log or power transform before it's fed into a model that's sensitive to extreme values — see [scaling & transformations](#scaling--transformations)
- outliers show up on a boxplot or via z-scores/iqr; decide whether each is a data error (fix or remove) or a genuine extreme value (keep, but prefer robust scaling over standard scaling)
- check this per feature, not once for the whole dataset — a mix of symmetric, skewed, and categorical columns is the normal case, not the exception

## data type drives preprocessing choices

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| data type | examples | typical preprocessing | especially sensitive models |
|---|---|---|---|
| continuous, roughly symmetric | height, standardised lab values | standard scaling | distance-based models, regularised linear models, neural networks |
| continuous, skewed | income, gene expression counts, time-to-event | log/power transform, then scale | same as above — skew distorts distances and gives extreme values outsized influence |
| ordinal | disease stage, education level | ordinal encoding that preserves order | any model — one-hot encoding would discard the order information |
| nominal / unordered categorical | blood type, tissue type | one-hot or target encoding | linear and distance-based models need a numeric encoding; tree models can often split on raw categories directly |
| count data | number of mutations, event counts | log1p transform, or a poisson/negative-binomial loss instead of squared error | ordinary least squares assumes gaussian errors, which small or zero-inflated counts violate |
| binary | yes/no, case/control | leave as 0/1 | — |

:::

- which model is about to run matters as much as the data itself does: [naive bayes](../supervised-learning/naive-bayes.qmd) assumes a specific distribution per feature (gaussian for continuous features, multinomial for counts) — mismatching that assumption weakens its probability estimates even when the final classification still looks reasonable
- [linear and logistic regression](../supervised-learning/linear-regression.qmd) don't require normally distributed *features*, only roughly gaussian *residuals* — but a skewed or heavy-tailed feature can still create outsized leverage and a poorly conditioned fit, see [residuals, leverage & influence](bias-variance.qmd#residuals-leverage--influence)
- distance-based models (k-nearest neighbours, k-means) and anything trained with gradient descent or [regularisation](regularisation.qmd) are directly sensitive to feature scale, since both distance calculations and penalty terms treat every feature's units as comparable — see [distance metrics](../foundations/distance-metrics.qmd#practical-considerations)
- tree-based models (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting) split on per-feature thresholds, so monotonic transforms like scaling or log transforms don't change their splits — distributional shape and scale matter far less there than for the models above

## missing data

- check how much is missing and why; in omics, an undetected measurement may reflect a detection limit
- dropping incomplete rows loses data and may introduce bias; a small missing percentage alone does not make deletion safe
- mean, median, or mode imputation is a simple baseline, but can distort variability and relationships
- knn imputation uses similar samples; chained-equation methods predict missing values from other features. multiple imputation creates several completed datasets to reflect uncertainty
- consider a missingness indicator when the fact that a value is missing may be informative

## categorical variables

- ordinal encoding represents categories with a meaningful order, such as disease stage
- one-hot encoding represents unordered categories without imposing a numeric order; many categories can create many columns
- target encoding uses target statistics for each category; use cross-fitting within the training data to avoid leakage
- embeddings learn compact representations of categories with many possible values

## scaling & transformations

- standard scaling: subtract the training mean and divide by its standard deviation, $x'=(x-\mu)/\sigma$
- min–max scaling: map training values to a chosen range; extreme values can dominate the scale
- robust scaling: centre using the median and scale using the interquartile range
- log and power transformations can reduce skew; they do not guarantee normally distributed data
- scaling matters for distance-based and many regularised or gradient-based models; ordinary decision trees generally do not need it

## feature selection & extraction

- filter methods: remove low-variance features or rank them using univariate statistics, such as mutual information
- wrapper methods: select subsets using a model, such as recursive feature elimination or forward/backward selection
- embedded methods: select features during fitting, such as l1 regularisation; tree importance can inform selection but needs validation
- selection keeps original variables; extraction creates new representations, such as [principal components](../dimensionality-reduction/pca.qmd)

## avoiding leakage

- split the data before fitting imputers, encoders, scalers, or feature selectors
- learn preprocessing only from the training set, then apply it to validation and test sets
- during cross-validation, refit preprocessing within each training fold; a pipeline helps enforce this
- related: [curse of dimensionality](../foundations/curse-of-dimensionality.qmd)
